question: A salesperson decides to leave their sponsoring broker and affiliate with a new firm. Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-19(b), what must the releasing broker do with that licensee's license?
choice_a: Immediately forward the license to GREC or to the new broker, and notify GREC of the termination with the required details
choice_b: Hold the license indefinitely until any disputed commission is resolved between the broker and the departing licensee
choice_c: Destroy the license, since a new one will be issued automatically to the new firm
choice_d: Forward the license only if the departing licensee has no pending transactions
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-19(b) requires the releasing broker to immediately forward the departing licensee's license to GREC or the new broker, and to notify GREC of the termination with the required details -- the broker may not simply hold the license as leverage over unrelated disputes.

question: A salesperson has left their broker but has not yet personally delivered a transfer application to GREC or received a new wall certificate. Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-19(b), may that salesperson continue engaging in real estate activities in the interim?
choice_a: Yes -- the licensee may continue practicing under the old broker's authority indefinitely until the new paperwork clears
choice_b: No -- the departing licensee cannot engage in real estate activities until either personally delivering a transfer application to GREC or receiving a wall certificate authorizing them under the new broker
choice_c: Yes -- the licensee may practice independently, without any broker affiliation, during the transition period
choice_d: Yes, but only for transactions that were already pending before the departure
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-19(b) provides that a departing licensee may not engage in real estate activities until either personally delivering a transfer application to GREC or receiving a wall certificate authorizing them as licensed under the new broker or qualifying broker.

question: A licensee transfers to a new firm but has several pending transactions originated under the former broker. Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-19(c), what must happen for the licensee to continue representing the former broker on those specific pending transactions?
choice_a: Nothing further is required -- the licensee may automatically continue on any pending matter without any documentation
choice_b: Only the departing licensee's personal consent is needed, with no involvement from either broker
choice_c: The former and new brokers must agree in writing, list the specific pending transactions, have the former broker assume responsibility for them, and document the compensation terms
choice_d: GREC must issue a special order authorizing continued representation in every such case
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-19(c) allows a transferring licensee to continue representing the former broker on pre-transfer transactions only if both brokers agree in writing, the specific transactions are listed, the former broker assumes responsibility, and the compensation terms are documented -- an ad hoc or undocumented continuation is not permitted.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-19(d), may a salesperson or community association manager act as a licensee for more than one broker at the same time?
choice_a: Yes -- salespersons may freely split their affiliation between multiple brokers without any special procedure
choice_b: Yes, but only associate brokers (not salespersons) face this restriction
choice_c: No such restriction exists under Georgia license law
choice_d: No -- a salesperson or CAM may not act as a licensee for any broker other than the broker holding their license, except as permitted under the § 43-40-19(c) pending-transaction procedure
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-19(d) provides that a salesperson or community association manager may not act as a licensee for any broker other than the one holding their license, except as permitted under the documented pending-transaction procedure in § 43-40-19(c).

question: A qualifying broker personally reviews a batch of listing contracts on day 45 after their contract dates, having missed the statutory review window entirely. Beyond the review-timing violation itself, what broader supervisory-procedure concern does this pattern most directly suggest?
choice_a: That the broker's supervisory procedures for timely contract review, required under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(c), may not be functioning as required, independent of whether any individual licensee also committed a separate violation
choice_b: No concern at all, since only the 90-day trust-fund examination window is legally significant
choice_c: That the broker should immediately dissolve the firm and reapply for a new license
choice_d: That only the individual licensees who signed those contracts, and not the broker, bear any responsibility
explanation: Consistently missing the 30-day contract-review window required by O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(c) suggests the broker's supervisory procedures themselves may be inadequate -- a distinct concern from any individual licensee's conduct, since the broker's own compliance with the enumerated supervisory duties is independently assessed.

question: As a matter of general national real estate brokerage practice (not a Georgia-specific statutory term), what is a 'broker-in-charge' or 'branch manager' role typically used for in a multi-office firm?
choice_a: A title with no supervisory function, used purely for marketing purposes
choice_b: A person to whom the qualifying broker delegates day-to-day supervisory functions at a given office location, while the qualifying broker retains ultimate statutory responsibility for that delegate's supervisory acts
choice_c: A position that fully replaces the qualifying broker's legal responsibility for that office
choice_d: A role reserved exclusively for community association managers
explanation: As a matter of general industry practice (consistent with, though not itself defined by, O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(d)'s delegation provision), a branch manager or 'broker-in-charge' role is commonly used to handle day-to-day office-level supervision, while the qualifying broker retains ultimate statutory responsibility for the delegate's supervisory acts.
source_note: hedge: standard national brokerage-practice terminology, consistent with O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(d)'s delegation rule

question: A qualifying broker allows an unlicensed personal assistant to negotiate price terms directly with a buyer on the broker's behalf. What supervisory concern does this raise under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(c)?
choice_a: No concern -- unlicensed assistants may perform any task a broker delegates to them
choice_b: It is permitted as long as the assistant is a family member of the broker
choice_c: It conflicts with the required supervisory procedure ensuring that only licensed personnel perform acts requiring a license -- negotiating price terms is a licensable activity an unlicensed assistant may not lawfully perform
choice_d: It is a concern only if the assistant is paid a commission-based fee for the negotiation
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(c) requires supervisory procedures ensuring only licensed personnel perform licensable acts; negotiating price terms with a buyer on the broker's behalf is a licensable brokerage activity, so allowing an unlicensed assistant to do so undermines this required supervisory safeguard regardless of the assistant's relationship to the broker or fee arrangement.

question: A firm's qualifying broker dies unexpectedly. Under Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 520-1-.07(3), does the firm's 60-day window to secure a replacement qualifying broker apply the same way it would to a resignation or discharge?
choice_a: No -- death of a qualifying broker automatically and permanently dissolves the firm's license with no replacement window at all
choice_b: No -- death extends the window to a full calendar year, unlike resignation or discharge
choice_c: No -- death of a qualifying broker is not addressed by Georgia rule at all
choice_d: Yes -- Rule 520-1-.07(3) applies the same 60-day replacement window regardless of whether the qualifying broker's departure was by death, resignation, or discharge
explanation: Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 520-1-.07(3) treats death, resignation, and discharge of the qualifying broker the same way for purposes of the 60-day replacement window -- the firm must secure a new qualifying broker within that period regardless of which of the three events triggered the vacancy, or it must cease brokerage activity.

question: Two different affiliated licensees at the same firm each separately violate license law within the same month, and the broker had documented, reasonable supervisory procedures covering both areas of violation, did not participate in either violation, and did not ratify either. Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(b), does having two separate violations by two different licensees change the safe-harbor analysis?
choice_a: No -- the safe-harbor analysis under § 43-40-18(b) is applied on the same three-element basis (reasonable procedures, no participation, no ratification) regardless of how many separate affiliate violations occur
choice_b: Yes -- a second unrelated violation within the same month automatically forfeits the safe harbor regardless of the broker's conduct
choice_c: Yes -- the broker must personally re-certify supervisory procedures to GREC after each individual violation to preserve the defense
choice_d: No, because Georgia law caps the safe harbor at one violation per firm per year
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(b)'s three-element safe-harbor test (reasonable supervisory procedures, no participation, no ratification) applies to each instance of an affiliate's violation on its own terms; the statute does not impose a cap on the number of separate affiliate violations a broker may successfully defend against under the same three-element showing.
